link.title: Reading Notes of Huxley-Gödel Machine: Human-Level Coding Agent Development by an Approximation of the Optimal Self-Improving Machine

entry.content:
TL;DR: A “better” scorer for evaluating coding agents.

Reference: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.21614

Key terms (read first)

Term Meaning
LLM (large language model) A neural network that generates text and code, e.g., GPT-5, GPT-5-mini, Qwen3-Coder.
Coding agent A program (a “scaffold”) that wraps an LLM in a loop with tools such as a shell (bash) and a file editor, so it can read a code repository, edit files, run tests, and submit a fix. The LLM stays fixed; the agent’s own code is what changes in this paper.
Benchmark, task, accuracy A benchmark is a fixed set of coding problems (tasks). Hidden tests mark each attempt as pass (1) or fail (0). Accuracy is the fraction of tasks passed.
SWE-bench Verified / Lite Real GitHub issues from 12 popular Python repositories; the agent must write a code patch that makes hidden tests pass. Verified has 500 human-checked tasks; Lite has 300 tasks, 93 of which also appear in Verified. SWE-Verified-60 is a 60-task subset of Verified.
Polyglot A benchmark of programming exercises in C++, Java, Python, Go, Rust, and JavaScript, from the Aider coding-assistant project.
Self-modification An agent edits a copy of its own source code. The edited copy is its child; the original is the parent.
Archive tree, clade All agents created so far, linked parent → child, form a tree. The clade of an agent is that agent plus all of its descendants (its subtree). The word comes from biologist Julian Huxley: a lineage sharing one common ancestor.
Metaproductivity How good an agent is at producing better future agents, as opposed to how good it is at solving tasks itself.
Gödel Machine A theoretical self-rewriting program (Schmidhuber, 2003) that changes its own code only after proving that the change raises expected long-term utility. It is optimal in principle but needs formal proofs.
DGM, SICA Darwin Gödel Machine and Self-Improving Coding Agent: the two prior self-improving coding-agent systems that HGM is compared against.
SWE-agent A leading human-designed coding agent; it serves as the human reference.
Bayesian / Thompson sampling Choosing among options by drawing one random plausible success rate per option from a belief distribution and taking the largest draw (made precise in the Math section).
Allocated CPU-hours CPU cores reserved × wall-clock hours; the paper’s measure of compute cost.
Checked leaderboard results SWE-bench leaderboard entries whose results the benchmark maintainers have verified.

Summary

Self-improving coding agents (LLM programs that fix bugs) rewrite their own code, growing a family tree of versions; which to modify next? Prior methods pick the top benchmark scorer, but strong scorers can have weak descendants. The Huxley–Gödel Machine (HGM) rates each agent by pooled test success across its subtree (“clade”) and chooses what to modify or test by Bayesian sampling. On SWE-bench Verified and Polyglot: (1) clade scores predict descendants’ best far better; (2) HGM finds stronger agents with 2.4–6.9× fewer CPU-hours than DGM; (3) its GPT-5-mini-optimized agent, run with GPT-5, matches top human-designed agents on SWE-bench Lite.

Motivation

Agents that improve their own improvement process could compound progress without human redesign. The Gödel Machine accepts only self-edits it can prove beneficial: optimal, but proofs are impractical. DGM and SICA instead edit the agents with the highest benchmark scores. This fails because a score measures current skill, not the quality of future descendants (the Metaproductivity–Performance Mismatch); scores from few tests are noisy; and testing every new child immediately wastes budget. HGM judges agents by their descendants’ results, the quantity the Gödel Machine optimizes. The motivation is clear; its empirical evidence is correlational, from one run per method.

Math

(a) Prerequisites

Notation used throughout (simplified from the paper; the paper’s $n_{\text{success}}(a)$ is $s(a)$ here, and its clade sum $n^{C}_{\text{success}}(a)$ is $S(a)$):

Symbol Meaning
$a$, $a_0$ an agent; the initial (root) agent
$\mathcal{T}_t$ the archive tree after step $t$; $\lvert\mathcal{T}_t\rvert$ is its number of agents
$\mathcal{C}(a)$ the clade of $a$: $a$ plus all its descendants
$\mathcal{D}$ the task set (benchmark)
$U(a)\in[0,1]$ the true accuracy of agent $a$ on $\mathcal{D}$ (its utility)
$s(a)$, $f(a)$ passes and fails observed for agent $a$ itself
$S(a)$, $F(a)$ passes and fails summed over every agent in $\mathcal{C}(a)$
$N_t$ total number of single agent–task tests done so far
$B$, $b$ total budget and remaining budget
$\pi$ the search policy, i.e., the algorithm (SICA, DGM, or HGM)

P1 — Empirical accuracy. Intuition: each test of agent $a$ is a coin flip whose unknown bias is $U(a)$; the share of heads estimates the bias.

\[\hat{p}(a)=\frac{s(a)}{s(a)+f(a)}\]

Example: 6 passes and 4 fails give $\hat{p}=6/10=0.6$.

P2 — Beta belief (posterior). Intuition: instead of a single number, keep a whole belief curve over the unknown success rate. A posterior is the belief after seeing data. It starts flat and narrows as tests accumulate. Starting from the flat $\mathrm{Beta}(1,1)$, after $s$ passes and $f$ fails the belief is $\mathrm{Beta}(1+s,\,1+f)$.

\[p\sim\mathrm{Beta}(x,y),\qquad \mathbb{E}[p]=\frac{x}{x+y},\qquad \mathrm{Var}[p]=\frac{xy}{(x+y)^2(x+y+1)}\]

Example: 3 passes, 7 fails → $\mathrm{Beta}(4,8)$: mean $4/12\approx0.333$, variance $32/(144\cdot13)\approx0.0171$, standard deviation $\approx0.131$.

P3 — Thompson sampling. Intuition: let every option “roll” a plausible success rate from its belief and pick the highest roll. A well-tested strong option wins most rounds; a barely tested option wins some rounds, which keeps exploring it.

\[\theta_i\sim\mathrm{Beta}(x_i,y_i)\ \text{for each option } i,\qquad \text{choose } \arg\max_i\theta_i\]

Example: option A has $\mathrm{Beta}(4,8)$ (mean 0.33, well tested), option B has $\mathrm{Beta}(2,2)$ (mean 0.5, barely tested). One round draws $\theta_A=0.29$, $\theta_B=0.71$ → B. Another round draws $0.41$ and $0.35$ → A.

P4 — Bandits. A multi-armed bandit is a row of slot machines (“arms”) with unknown payout rates; each pull reveals one outcome. In an infinite-armed bandit you may also add brand-new machines. Here an arm is an agent, a pull is one test of that agent on one task, and adding an arm is creating a new agent by self-modification.

P5 — Q-value and Bellman optimality. Intuition: the Q-value of an action is the expected final payoff if you take that action now and then keep following policy $\pi$. Bellman optimality says that always taking the action with the larger Q-value (under the best continuation) is the optimal strategy.

\[Q^{\pi}(\text{state},x)=\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\big[\text{final reward}\mid\text{take action } x \text{ now}\big]\]

Example: “accept” leads to final reward 0.6 or 0.4 with equal chance, so $Q=0.5$; “reject” leads to 0.45 for sure, so $Q=0.45$. Accept.

P6 — POMDP. A partially observable Markov decision process is a sequential decision problem in which the decision-maker sees only part of the true state.

(b) Problem setup

Setting 1 — Self-improvement as tree search (all experiments).

  • Input: an initial agent $a_0$; a self-modification LLM that writes code edits to agents; a task-solving LLM that powers every agent while it attempts benchmark tasks; a benchmark $\mathcal{D}$; a budget $B$ counted in single agent–task tests (800 or 8000 in the experiments).
  • Each step, the policy takes one action: expand$(a)$ — agent $a$ rewrites a copy of its own code, and the copy joins the tree as $a$’s child; or evaluate$(a)$ — run $a$ on one task it has not tried and record pass or fail.
  • Output: when the budget is spent, the policy returns $a_{\text{final}}=\arg\max_{a\in\mathcal{T}_B}\mathrm{Score}(a)$ for its own scoring rule.
  • Objective. Intuition: the expected true accuracy of the agent you hand in at the end.
\[J(\pi)=\mathbb{E}\big[U(a_{\text{final}})\big]\]

Example: if a method hands in an agent of true accuracy 0.55 in half of its possible runs and 0.60 in the other half, $J=0.575$.

  • How performance is measured: the accuracy of $a_{\text{final}}$ on the benchmark, plus the compute spent (allocated CPU-hours).
  • Reference points: the initial agent, DGM and SICA under the same test budget, and the human-designed SWE-agent.
  • Out of scope: training or fine-tuning LLM weights (only agent code changes), rewards collected before the end, the general time-aware Gödel Machine, and the safety of executing self-written code.

Setting 2 — The Gödel Machine game (theory only). The paper’s Assumption 1:

  1. Only the final agent matters; there is no reward before the end.
  2. Repeatable trials: an agent’s expected result on a task does not depend on when it is tested or what happened before (each test runs in a freshly reset environment).
  3. The Gödel Machine’s prover knows the utility function, and proofs cost no budget.
  4. Each self-modification costs exactly one budget unit, and the budget is finite and known.

Game: the state is (tree, current parent $p$, newest child $c$, remaining budget $b$); the decision-maker observes only $(p, c, b)$. Each step it chooses accept ($c$ becomes the parent) or reject ($p$ stays the parent); the new parent then produces a fresh child, and $b$ drops by one. When $b=0$ it outputs $p$ or $c$, and the reward is $U$ of that output.

Setting 3 — Transfer test (final experiments). No search: the finished agent is run on SWE-bench Lite, optionally with its task-solving LLM swapped from GPT-5-mini to GPT-5.

(c) Evaluation metrics

M1 — Accuracy (Settings 1 and 3). Intuition: the share of benchmark tasks the agent solves; this is what the whole search tries to maximize.

\[\mathrm{Acc}(a)=\frac{1}{\lvert\mathcal{D}\rvert}\sum_{d\in\mathcal{D}}\mathbb{1}\big[a\text{ solves }d\big]\]

Example: 34 of 60 tasks solved → 56.7%.

M2 — Allocated CPU-hours. Intuition: how much compute the run reserved to finish its budget; lower means cheaper and faster. CPU-hours $=$ cores reserved $\times$ wall-clock hours. Example: 8 cores for 40 hours = 320 CPU-hours.

M3 — Empirical CMP (the target for estimator quality). Intuition: after a run ends, ask “how good did this agent’s family actually get?” by taking the best observed accuracy among its descendants (excluding the agent itself).

\[\mathrm{CMP}^{\mathrm{emp}}(a)=\max_{a'\in\mathcal{C}(a)\setminus\{a\}}\hat{p}(a')\]

Example: $a$’s descendants scored 0.45, 0.58, and 0.52 → $\mathrm{CMP}^{\mathrm{emp}}(a)=0.58$.

M4 — Guidance scores being tested. SICA and DGM guide the search with an agent’s own accuracy $\hat{p}(a)$. HGM’s guide is its clade estimate (defined in part f), tested in a leak-free form. Intuition: pool the clade’s results but remove (i) $a$’s own tests and (ii) the whole branch that contains the best descendant, so the predictor never sees the answer it is predicting. Let $b^{\star}$ be the child of $a$ whose clade contains $a$’s best-scoring descendant.

\[\widehat{\mathrm{CMP}}^{\,\mathrm{lf}}(a)=\frac{S(a)-s(a)-S(b^{\star})}{\big[S(a)+F(a)\big]-\big[s(a)+f(a)\big]-\big[S(b^{\star})+F(b^{\star})\big]}\]

Example: $a$ itself is 2/5; child $b_1$’s clade (holding the best descendant) totals 12 passes and 8 fails; child $b_2$’s clade totals 6 passes and 4 fails. Then $S(a)=20$, $F(a)=15$, and the estimate is $(20-2-12)/(35-5-20)=6/10=0.6$, i.e., only $b_2$’s branch is used.

M5 — Pearson correlation (unweighted and weighted). Intuition: does the guidance score rise when the target rises? $+1$ is perfect agreement, $0$ is none, $-1$ is opposite. The weighted version counts each agent by the number of tests $w_i$ behind its prediction, so well-supported predictions matter more; the unweighted version uses $w_i=1$.

\[r_w=\frac{\sum_i w_i(x_i-\bar{x}_w)(y_i-\bar{y}_w)}{\sqrt{\sum_i w_i(x_i-\bar{x}_w)^2}\,\sqrt{\sum_i w_i(y_i-\bar{y}_w)^2}},\qquad \bar{x}_w=\frac{\sum_i w_ix_i}{\sum_i w_i}\]

Here $x_i$ is the guidance score of agent $i$ and $y_i$ its empirical CMP. Example (unweighted): $x=(0.2,0.4,0.6)$, $y=(0.3,0.5,0.4)$. Both means are 0.4; deviations are $(-0.2,0,0.2)$ and $(-0.1,0.1,0)$. Then $r=0.02/\sqrt{0.08\times0.02}=0.02/0.04=0.5$.

M6 — SWE-bench Lite, filtered vs. standard. Filtered drops the 93 tasks shared with SWE-bench Verified, leaving 207 tasks the agent never saw during search; it measures pure transfer. Standard uses all 300 tasks, matching the public leaderboard. Example: 40.1% on filtered ≈ 83 of 207 tasks.

(d) The standard approach and why it fails

The standard rule is “greedy by score”: pick the current best scorer as the parent, then test its new child on a batch of tasks. Intuition: bet on whoever performs best today.

\[a_{\text{parent}}=\arg\max_{a\in\mathcal{T}_t}\hat{p}(a)\]

Example: agent A scores 0.55 and agent B scores 0.45, so the rule keeps expanding A.

  • Failure F1 — Metaproductivity–Performance Mismatch. The right quantity for choosing a parent is how good its descendants become, not $\hat{p}(a)$. Example: A’s children score 0.50, 0.52, 0.48 (best 0.52); B’s children score 0.58, 0.60 (best 0.60). The greedy rule keeps feeding A.
  • Failure F2 — Noise. With few tests, $\hat{p}$ is unreliable: a lucky 3/3 (1.00) outranks a solid 30/50 (0.60).
  • Failure F3 — Rigid budget use. Every new child receives its batch of tests even after failing nine in a row, while older promising agents receive none.
  • Failure F4 — Sequential execution. Modification and testing wait on each other, so hardware sits idle and runs take long.

(e) Existing baselines

Method Which agent to modify Which agent to test What it fixes What remains
SICA The best scorer so far (greedy), with the full history of past attempts in its prompt The newest agent, on the entire dataset Gives a simple, working self-improvement loop; the history helps the LLM learn from past edits F1–F4 all remain; the growing history overflows the LLM’s context window (it stalled after 360 of 800 tests on SWE-Verified-60)
DGM A random agent from the archive, with a weight that grows with its score and shrinks with how many children it already has The newest agent, progressively: a small batch first, more tasks only if promising Keeps every agent (an open-ended archive) and explores beyond the single best; partial early stopping (part of F3) Still ranks by an agent’s own score (F1), small noisy batches (F2), newest-child-first testing (F3), sequential (F4)

(f) The HGM pipeline

One-sentence idea. Rate each agent by how well its entire family of descendants performs, and use Bayesian sampling to decide, one test at a time, whether to create a new agent or test an existing one, and which.

Analogy. Progeny testing in animal breeding: a breeding bull is ranked by the milk yield of his daughters, not by his own appearance. HGM ranks an agent by its descendants’ test results, not by its own score.

Step 1 — The ideal target: clade-metaproductivity (CMP). Intuition: “If I expand agent $a$ now and keep growing the tree until the budget runs out, how good will the best member of $a$’s family be?” Let $\mathcal{T}B$ be the final tree produced by expanding $a$ now and then following $\pi$, and $\mathcal{C}{\mathcal{T}_B}(a)$ be $a$’s clade in that final tree.

\[\mathrm{CMP}^{\pi}(\mathcal{T},a)=\mathbb{E}_{\mathcal{T}_B\sim\pi}\Big[\max_{a'\in\mathcal{C}_{\mathcal{T}_B}(a)}U(a')\Big]\]

Example: two equally likely futures in which the best family member has accuracy 0.60 or 0.50 → $\mathrm{CMP}=0.55$. (The paper also defines a global version, GMP, that takes the best agent in the whole final tree; GMP is the exact Q-value of “expand $a$” but is too broad to estimate. CMP narrows attention to $a$’s own subtree.)

Step 2 — Why CMP is the right target (Theorem 1). Assumptions: Assumption 1 (Setting 2). Result: access to the true CMP (an “oracle”) suffices to implement the Gödel Machine. Proof idea: in the Gödel game, once an agent is chosen as parent, every later agent descends from it, and the final output (last parent or last child) also lies in its clade. Hence “best final agent in $a$’s clade” equals “final reward of choosing $a$ now,” which is exactly the Q-value:

\[\mathrm{CMP}^{\pi}(\text{state},a)=Q^{\pi}(\text{state},a)\]

A Gödel Machine accepts a child only when it can prove that doing so yields higher expected utility, which is the same as comparing the CMP of child and parent (ties keep the parent). Choosing the larger Q-value is Bellman-optimal (P5). Example: $\mathrm{CMP}(\text{child})=0.58>\mathrm{CMP}(\text{parent})=0.55$ → accept; if both were 0.55 → keep the parent.

Step 3 — Estimate CMP by pooling the clade. Intuition: the true CMP is unknown, so pool every pass/fail recorded anywhere in $a$’s clade. This equals an average of the members’ accuracies weighted by how often each was tested. Because HGM tests strong agents more (Step 5), strong descendants carry more weight, so the pooled rate behaves like a soft maximum over the family.

\[\widehat{\mathrm{CMP}}(a)=\frac{S(a)}{S(a)+F(a)}=\sum_{a'\in\mathcal{C}(a)}\frac{n(a')}{\sum_{a''\in\mathcal{C}(a)}n(a'')}\,\hat{p}(a'),\qquad n(a')=s(a')+f(a')\]

Example: $a$ is 3/10, its child is 6/10, and its grandchild is 16/20. Pooled: $(3+6+16)/(10+10+20)=25/40=0.625$, while $a$’s own score is only 0.30. The heavily tested grandchild supplies half the weight.

Step 4 — Choose whom to expand: Thompson sampling on clade counts, sharpened over time. Intuition: each agent draws a plausible “family quality” from its clade belief, and the highest draw gets to self-modify. A schedule $\tau$ grows as the budget runs out: early draws are spread out (explore), late draws hug the means (exploit). Multiplying both Beta parameters by $\tau$ keeps the mean but shrinks the spread.

\[\theta_a\sim\mathrm{Beta}\big(\tau(1+S(a)),\,\tau(1+F(a))\big),\qquad a^{\star}_{\text{expand}}=\arg\max_a\theta_a,\qquad \tau=\frac{B}{b}\]

Example: $S=3$, $F=7$. At the start ($\tau=1$): $\mathrm{Beta}(4,8)$, mean 0.333, standard deviation 0.131. Halfway ($b=B/2$, $\tau=2$): $\mathrm{Beta}(8,16)$, same mean, standard deviation 0.094.

Step 5 — Choose whom to test: Thompson sampling on each agent’s own counts. Intuition: the same lottery, but on each agent’s own record, among agents that still have untried tasks; the winner is tested on one new task. Strong agents get tested often, which sharpens their estimates and makes them dominate their ancestors’ clade pools. Weak agents stop receiving tests after a few failures (early stopping).

\[\phi_a\sim\mathrm{Beta}\big(\tau(1+s(a)),\,\tau(1+f(a))\big),\qquad a^{\star}_{\text{eval}}=\arg\max_a\phi_a\]

After the test, add the pass or fail to $s$ or $f$ of $a^{\star}$, and to $S$ or $F$ of $a^{\star}$ and every one of its ancestors. Example: an agent at 0/9 has $\mathrm{Beta}(1,10)$ (mean 0.09); an agent at 5/10 has $\mathrm{Beta}(6,6)$ (mean 0.5). With $\tau=1$, the 0/9 agent wins the draw only about 0.9% of the time.

Step 6 — Expand or test? (widening rule from UCB-AIR). Intuition: UCB-AIR is an infinite-armed-bandit algorithm (Wang et al., 2008) that adds a new arm only when the number of pulls is large enough. HGM keeps the number of agents growing like a power of the number of tests, so the tree widens more slowly than evidence accumulates and each agent gets more tests over time.

\[\text{expand at step } t\iff N_t^{\alpha}\ge\lvert\mathcal{T}_t\rvert,\qquad \alpha=0.6\]

Example: after $N=100$ tests, $100^{0.6}\approx15.8$. A tree of 12 agents → expand; a tree of 16 → test. A run of 800 tests ends with about $800^{0.6}\approx55$ agents; a run of 8000 with about 220.

Step 7 — Hand in the best-belief agent. Intuition: return the agent whose pessimistic estimate is highest, so a lucky short streak cannot beat a long solid record. Let $q_{\epsilon}$ be the $\epsilon$-th percentile of a distribution (the value below which $\epsilon\%$ of it lies); the paper uses $\epsilon=1$, the 1st percentile.

\[a_{\text{final}}=\arg\max_{a}\;q_{\epsilon}\Big(\mathrm{Beta}\big(1+s(a),\,1+f(a)\big)\Big)\]

Example: agent X at 3/3 has $\mathrm{Beta}(4,1)$, whose 1st percentile is $0.01^{1/4}\approx0.32$. Agent Y at 30/50 has $\mathrm{Beta}(31,21)$ with mean 0.596 and standard deviation 0.067, so its 1st percentile is $\approx0.596-2.33\times0.067\approx0.44$. Y is handed in.

Step 8 — Run asynchronously. Several workers (20 in the released configuration) each run one iteration — an expansion or a test — and start the next iteration the moment they finish, using the latest counts. Jobs still running are counted when applying the Step 6 rule. The run opens with 5 expansions of the root agent executed in parallel, so early tests have several children to choose from. Easy tasks finish faster than hard ones, which makes early estimates slightly optimistic; the paper reports that this bias fades once an agent has about 50 tests.

Pseudocode.

Input: root a0, test budget B, alpha = 0.6, epsilon = 1 (percentile)
T <- {a0};  s, f, S, F <- 0 for every agent;  N <- 0
while N < B:                                  # every worker runs this loop concurrently
    tau <- B / (B - N)                        # sharpening schedule, grows toward the end
    if N^alpha >= |T|  (counting running jobs):          # widen the tree
        for each expandable agent a in T:                # code: agents with >= 1 pass
            theta_a ~ Beta(tau*(1+S(a)), tau*(1+F(a)))   # clade belief
        a* <- argmax theta_a
        child <- a* rewrites a copy of its own code      # self-modification LLM
        add child to T under a*
    else:                                                # gather evidence
        for each agent a in T with untried tasks:
            phi_a ~ Beta(tau*(1+s(a)), tau*(1+f(a)))     # own belief
        a* <- argmax phi_a
        r <- run a* on one untried task                  # task-solving LLM, r in {0,1}
        update s(a*) or f(a*); update S or F for a* and all its ancestors
        N <- N + 1
return argmax over a of 1st-percentile( Beta(1+s(a), 1+f(a)) )

How HGM fixes each failure.

Failure HGM’s fix
F1 Mismatch Parents are ranked by the clade estimate of CMP (Steps 3–4), the target that reproduces the Gödel Machine under Assumption 1 (Step 2).
F2 Noise Pooling over the clade gives each decision far more data; Beta beliefs and Thompson sampling account for uncertainty; the final pick is pessimistic (Step 7).
F3 Rigid budget Testing is decoupled from creation and happens one agent–task pair at a time (Steps 5–6), so weak agents stop being tested early.
F4 Sequential Workers run expansions and tests asynchronously (Step 8).

Results and Analysis

Organization. The experiments answer three questions in sequence. Part A checks the premise: does a guidance score predict how good an agent’s descendants become? (Table 1; metrics M3–M5.) Part B checks the payoff: does better guidance yield better agents with less compute? (Table 2; metrics M1–M2.) Part C checks scale and generality: when the search is scaled to the full SWE-bench Verified, does the resulting agent rival human designs and transfer to new tasks and a stronger LLM? (Tables 3–4; metrics M1, M6.) General setup: every HGM run uses the asynchronous version with $\tau=B/b$, $\epsilon=1$, and $\alpha=0.6$; HGM, DGM, and SICA all start from the same initial agent, taken from DGM’s code: a single LLM loop with a bash tool and a file-editing tool, with a one-hour limit per run of the agent. Budgets are counted in single agent–task tests. How to read the tables: in Table 1, columns are correlations in $[-1,1]$, and higher means the guidance score better tracks long-term self-improvement. In Table 2, the accuracy columns are better when higher (the “+” number is the gain over the initial agent), and the CPU-hours columns are better when lower. In Tables 3–4, columns are accuracy on SWE-bench Lite (filtered = 207 never-seen tasks; standard = all 300 tasks), higher is better. Task counts in parentheses are computed from the reported percentages.

Part A — Does the guidance score predict long-term self-improvement?

Question and setup. After each method finishes its search on SWE-Verified-60 and on Polyglot, the authors take every agent in its tree and compute the target, empirical CMP (M3: the best accuracy among its descendants). They correlate it with the method’s own guidance score (M4): an agent’s own accuracy for SICA and DGM, and the leak-free clade estimate for HGM. Correlations are reported unweighted and weighted by the number of tests behind each prediction (M5). How to read: around 0.3 means the score barely tells you which agents have productive descendants; around 0.8 means it tells you well.

Guidance score SWE-Verified-60, weighted SWE-Verified-60, unweighted Polyglot, weighted Polyglot, unweighted
SICA (own accuracy) 0.444 0.444 0.274 0.274
DGM (own accuracy) 0.285 0.406 0.383 0.357
HGM (clade estimate) 0.778 0.512 0.626 0.873

Takeaway 1 — An agent’s own score is a weak guide; the clade estimate is a strong one.

  • Own-accuracy scores correlate only 0.27–0.44 with descendants’ best result, which is the empirical face of the Metaproductivity–Performance Mismatch (failure F1).
  • HGM’s clade estimate reaches 0.78 (SWE-Verified-60) and 0.63 (Polyglot) weighted, and 0.51 and 0.87 unweighted — the highest in every column.
  • The weighted gain is largest on SWE-Verified-60 (0.778 vs. at most 0.444), showing that well-supported clade estimates are the most trustworthy ones.

Part B — Does better guidance give better agents with less compute?

Question and setup. Each method runs a budget of 800 tests. On SWE-Verified-60, GPT-5 writes the self-modifications and GPT-5-mini solves the tasks; on Polyglot, a quantized Qwen3-Coder-480B-A35B-Instruct writes the self-modifications and Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct solves the tasks. Agents see no hidden tests or test results on Polyglot. Every reported Polyglot percentage equals a whole number of tasks out of 59 (e.g., 30.5% = 18/59, 20.3% = 12/59), which matches the released code’s Polyglot subset rather than the full benchmark; this task count is inferred, not stated in the paper. The initial agent scores 40.0% (24/60) on SWE-Verified-60 and 20.3% on Polyglot. HGM hands in its best-belief agent; DGM and SICA hand in their agent with the highest observed accuracy. The total API cost for all three methods was about 5,000 USD. How to read: look for the method that is simultaneously highest in accuracy (M1) and lowest in CPU-hours (M2).

SICA 50.0 (+10.0), 30/60 did not finish (stalled after 360 tests) 25.4 (+5.1), ≈15/59 572

Takeaway 2 — HGM finds the strongest agent and uses the least compute.

  • Accuracy: HGM’s gain over the initial agent is +16.7 points on SWE-Verified-60 (DGM +13.3, SICA +10.0) and +10.2 on Polyglot (DGM +6.8, SICA +5.1).
  • Compute: HGM needs 2.38× fewer CPU-hours than DGM on SWE-Verified-60, and 6.86× fewer than DGM and 1.65× fewer than SICA on Polyglot. SICA’s run on SWE-Verified-60 stopped improving after 360 tests (45% of its budget) because its prompts exceeded the LLM’s context window.
  • Figure 1 (right) plots the best accuracy found against CPU-hours on SWE-Verified-60: HGM’s curve reaches 56.67% at ≈517 CPU-hours, while the DGM curve plateaus and runs to ≈1231 CPU-hours. The figure labels the two baseline values the other way around from Table 2 (DGM 50%, SICA 53.33%); with either labeling, HGM is highest.

Part C — Does the approach scale, rival human designs, and transfer?

Question and setup. The search is scaled to the full SWE-bench Verified (500 tasks) with 8000 tests, and GPT-5-mini solves the tasks. The initial agent is made stronger and less biased: it keeps only the bash tool (no file editor) and gets five-hour limits for both self-modification and task runs, which yields 53.2% to start. The best-belief agent is then tested on SWE-bench Lite (Setting 3) in two forms: with GPT-5-mini (Table 3) and with GPT-5 swapped in (Table 4). Comparisons are the initial ancestor; SWE-agent, the top human-designed agent with checked results, re-run by the authors with GPT-5-mini; and SWE-agent’s leaderboard-leading submission with Claude 4 Sonnet. How to read: the filtered column (M6) is the clean test of generalization; the standard column is what the public leaderboard shows.

Result on the optimization benchmark itself: SWE-bench Verified accuracy rises from 53.2% to 61.4%, the top GPT-5-mini system on the leaderboard and within the top 10 of all checked submissions, including systems on more expensive LLMs.

Table 3 — same LLM (GPT-5-mini), new tasks:

Agent SWE-Lite filtered, 207 tasks (%) SWE-Lite standard, 300 tasks (%)
HGM initial ancestor 34.8 (≈72) 44.0 (132)
SWE-agent + GPT-5-mini 39.6 (≈82) 47.6 (≈143)
HGM best-belief agent 40.1 (≈83) 49.0 (147)

Table 4 — stronger LLM (GPT-5) vs. the leaderboard leader:

Agent SWE-Lite filtered, 207 tasks (%) SWE-Lite standard, 300 tasks (%)
SWE-agent, leaderboard #1 (Claude 4 Sonnet) 48.3 (≈100) 56.7 (170)
HGM best-belief agent + GPT-5 47.8 (≈99) 57.0 (171)

Takeaway 3 — The evolved design generalizes across tasks and LLMs and reaches the level of the best human-designed agent.

  • New tasks: on the 207 never-seen tasks, the HGM agent beats its own ancestor by +5.3 points (40.1 vs. 34.8), so the search improved general coding ability rather than memorizing SWE-bench Verified. With the same GPT-5-mini, it also edges out SWE-agent (40.1 vs. 39.6; 49.0 vs. 47.6), which isolates the gain to agent design rather than the LLM. Its 49.0% standard score ranks second among checked SWE-bench Lite submissions.
  • New LLM: with GPT-5 swapped in, the agent scores 57.0% on standard SWE-bench Lite, one task above the leaderboard leader (56.7%) and the best among checked results; on the filtered set it is one task behind (47.8 vs. 48.3). This is the paper’s “human-level” claim.
  • Other observations: inspecting the evolved code shows self-written additions such as automatic error diagnosis after failed tests and multi-attempt test-and-revise loops, and some agents performed several self-edits within a single expansion step.

Limitations

The statistical evidence is thin relative to the strength of the claims. Every comparison is a single run per method with no repeated seeds or confidence intervals, even though LLM-driven self-modification is highly random. On SWE-Verified-60 one task is 1.7 points, so HGM’s lead over DGM is 34 vs. 32 tasks (and on the roughly 59-task Polyglot set, 18 vs. 16), and the SWE-bench Lite comparisons that support “human-level” are decided by one to four tasks, with the GPT-5 comparison winning by one task on the standard set and losing by one on the filtered set. The correlation study scores each estimator on its own method’s tree, so differences in tree shape and in how tests were allocated are mixed into the comparison of estimators. Figure 1 and Table 2 also assign the two baseline accuracies differently.

The theory justifies the target but not the estimator or the algorithm. Theorem 1 holds only under strong assumptions (repeatable trials, free proofs, unit-cost modifications, a game restricted to accepting or rejecting one child), and it is close to definitional: CMP is constructed to equal the Q-value in that game, so an oracle for it gives optimal decisions almost by construction. The practical algorithm departs from that game in several ways: it tests agents (an action the theorem removes), expands any agent in the tree, and runs asynchronously. Its estimator is a pooled mean rather than an expected maximum under the future policy, so its value depends on how tests happened to be allocated. No bound links the estimate to true CMP, so “approximates the Gödel Machine” is a design motivation rather than a guarantee.

The efficiency and generality claims mix algorithm with engineering and stay within one domain. Much of the CPU-hour saving comes from asynchronous parallel execution, which could be added to DGM and SICA as well, and the dominant real cost — LLM tokens and API spend per method — is not compared. The 61.4% result is measured on the same benchmark that guided the search and the final selection, so only the filtered SWE-bench Lite numbers are clean, and those tasks come from the same 12 Python repositories as SWE-bench Verified. All experiments concern coding agents improving their scaffolds on two benchmarks with two model families; the safety of agents that rewrite and execute their own code is left unstudied.

How to Reproduce

Step 1 — Get the code. The official implementation is at github.com/metauto-ai/HGM under the Apache-2.0 license and is built on the Darwin Gödel Machine codebase. The main entry point is hgm.py (with tree.py and hgm_utils.py for the tree search), agent code lives in coding_agent.py and coding_agent_polyglot.py, settings live in config.yaml, and a best_agent/ folder holds the released discovered agent, which lets you reproduce the transfer results without rerunning the search.

Step 2 — Build the environment. Create a Python 3.10 conda environment and install requirements.txt; install Docker and confirm your user can run containers, because every task runs inside a container; export OPENAI_API_KEY. The provided run.sh activates an environment named agent while the README creates one named hgm, so align the two names. The repository executes untrusted, model-generated code, so run it on an isolated machine.

Step 3 — Prepare the benchmarks. Clone SWE-bench into swe_bench/ at the commit pinned in the README and install it in editable mode; build the Polyglot data with python -m polyglot.prepare_polyglot_dataset (git must have a user name and email configured). By default hgm.py searches on swe_bench/subsets/small.json + medium.json, which is SWE-Verified-60 (DGM’s first two evaluation stages), and on polyglot/subsets/small.json + medium.json for Polyglot; with --full_eval it loads all 500 tasks of princeton-nlp/SWE-bench_Verified from Hugging Face. The initial agent is first tested on every search task, and those tests do not count toward the budget. For the filtered SWE-bench Lite evaluation, remove the 93 instance IDs that also appear in SWE-bench Verified to obtain the 207-task set.

Step 4 — Match the paper’s settings. The released config.yaml sets alpha: 0.6, max_task_evals: 800, max_workers: 20, one-hour timeouts, and GPT-5-mini for self-modification, task solving, and failure diagnosis; every option also has a command-line flag. The paper’s sharpening schedule $\tau=B/b$ is the cool_down option with beta: 1.0 (the code multiplies both Beta parameters by $B^{\beta}/(B-N)^{\beta}$); it ships switched off, so pass --cool_down to match the paper. For the SWE-Verified-60 comparison, pass --self_improve_llm with GPT-5. For Polyglot, pass --polyglot and serve Qwen3-Coder-480B-A35B-Instruct (int4/int8 mixed quantization made with Intel’s AutoRound) and Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct behind an endpoint that llm.py can call. For the full-Verified run, pass --full_eval --max_task_evals 8000, set both timeouts to 18000 seconds, and point --initial_agent_name at a bash-only initial agent built as described in Appendix C.1.

Step 5 — Run the search. Launch ./run.sh, which cleans up Docker and calls python hgm.py (add the flags from Step 4 to that call); results go to output_hgm/<run_id>/, where hgm_metadata.jsonl records every agent’s parent and its pass/fail history. The search loop itself does not pick the final agent, so apply the best-belief rule (Step 7 of the pipeline: highest 1st percentile of $\mathrm{Beta}(1+s,1+f)$) to those records. Expect hundreds of allocated CPU-hours per 800-test run (517 for HGM on SWE-Verified-60) and API spending on the order of the paper’s roughly 5,000 USD across all three methods.

Step 6 — Evaluate and compare. Score the handed-in agent with evaluate_agent.py on SWE-bench Verified and on SWE-bench Lite (filtered and standard), then swap the task-solving LLM to GPT-5 for the transfer test. For baselines, run DGM from github.com/jennyzzt/dgm, SICA from the code released with Robeyns et al. (2025), and SWE-agent using its Claude 4 Sonnet leaderboard configuration with GPT-5-mini substituted as the backbone.

Parts the paper and repository leave unspecified. Random seeds and run-to-run variance; how allocated CPU-hours were counted for each method and how many cores the baselines used; the exact task-ID lists for SWE-Verified-60 and filtered SWE-bench Lite; which LLM writes self-modifications in the full-Verified run and which LLM performs failure diagnosis in each experiment; the meaning of the option n_pseudo_descendant_evals (set to 10000 and passed into the clade-count computation), which the paper does not describe; a ready-made script for the best-belief selection; scripts for the correlation analysis of Part A (Appendix D gives the formulas); the search trees and logs of the reported runs; the Qwen serving setup; and the exact SWE-agent + GPT-5-mini configuration.

link.title: Reading Notes of Context Language Models

entry.content:
TL;DR: The LLM can freely treat its context as a file to edit it with code, so the model decides what to keep, compress, or delete.

Reference: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2609.37725

1. Summary

Language-model agents struggle on long tasks because their context—the text the model rereads at every step—only grows until it overflows. The paper introduces Context Language Models (CLMs): the context is mirrored into a file the model freely edits with code, so the model decides what to keep, compress, or delete. (1) Used as-is, CLMs beat fixed compression rules with less compute (web-research benchmark BrowseComp-Plus, Qwen3.6-27B: +11.4% relative accuracy, −21.5% compute); (2) the skill is learnable—trial-and-reward training lifts Qwen3.5-9B from 28.8% to 42.5%; (3) Suffix Cache Reuse, which recycles stored computation after edits, cuts server compute 35% at equal accuracy.

2. Motivation

Long agent tasks, like hours of coding, produce far more text than a model’s context window (its maximum readable length). Existing systems let the harness (the fixed program around the model) summarize at preset lengths, or give the model a few predefined tools (summarize, move to disk, read back). Both hard-code human guesses, so they lose details, cannot update text in place, and cannot remove text already read. Following the Bitter Lesson (general learned methods beat hand-designed ones), the paper grants unrestricted editing. One gap: it argues for full freedom by analogy and never tests partially restricted editing.

3. Math

(a) Prerequisites

  • Token: a word piece; models read and write tokens (1K tokens ≈ 750 English words).
  • Language model (LM) \(\pi_\theta\): a neural network with weights \(\theta\) that reads a token sequence and generates new tokens.
  • Context \(c\): the whole token sequence the LM reads in one call (instructions, past actions, tool outputs); \(\lvert c\rvert\) is its length.
  • Context budget \(B\): the largest allowed \(\lvert c\rvert\); mostly \(B = 32{,}768\) (“32K”) tokens here.
  • Agent, turn, harness: an agent is an LM acting in a loop. At turn \(t\) it reads \(c_t\), writes \(y_t\) (reasoning plus a shell command), and the environment returns an observation \(o_t\) (the command’s output). The harness is the program that runs this loop and assembles each context.
  • Compaction / offloading / retrieval: replacing old context by a shorter summary / moving text from the context to a disk file / reading it back.
  • Prefill and decode: prefill processes the prompt tokens in one parallel pass; decode generates new tokens one at a time.
  • KV cache and prefix caching: during prefill the model stores, for every token, a “key” and a “value” vector (the KV cache) that later tokens look back at. Prefix caching reuses the stored KV cache for the longest leading stretch of a new prompt that is identical to an earlier prompt; every token after the first difference is recomputed (“re-prefilled”).
  • Attention: the operation in which each token looks at all earlier tokens; its cost grows with the number of token pairs, i.e., quadratically with length.
  • RoPE (rotary position encoding): the model marks a token’s position by rotating its key vector by an angle proportional to that position.
  • Linear attention (Gated DeltaNet): a layer type that compresses all past tokens into one fixed-size state updated token by token, instead of storing per-token keys and values. Qwen3.6-27B uses it in 48 of its 64 layers; the other 16 are full-attention layers.
  • FLOPs / PFLOPs: floating-point operations, a hardware-independent count of compute; 1 PFLOP \(=10^{15}\) FLOPs.
  • Zero-shot: used as-is, without task-specific training.
  • Skill: a natural-language instruction document placed in the context.
  • Reinforcement learning (RL): training by sampling attempts and making highly rewarded attempts more likely.
Symbol Meaning
\(t\) turn index, \(t=1,\dots,T\)
\(c_t\) context at turn \(t\)
\(y_t,\ o_t\) model output and environment observation at turn \(t\)
\(\oplus\) concatenation (append)
\(B\) context budget in tokens
\(\pi_\theta\) the LM with weights \(\theta\)
\(s\) skill document
\(r\) task reward or score

(b) Problem setup

Every setting shares one loop: a task \(x\) arrives; for \(t=1,\dots,T\) the model reads \(c_t\), writes \(y_t \sim \pi_\theta(\cdot \mid c_t)\), and receives \(o_t\), with \(\lvert c_t\rvert \le B\) at every call. The goal is a high final score \(r\) at low total compute. The settings differ in task and reference:

Setting Input What is scored Reference
Coding and deep research (one agent, ≤100 turns) a terminal task, or a hard question plus a search tool over a fixed corpus pass rate; answer accuracy the task’s test script; an LLM judge holding the gold answer
Open discovery (hours to a day) an optimization problem or a code repository plus an evaluator best score reached automatic evaluator or benchmark judge
Multi-agent \(N\) agents, each with its own context \(c^{(1)},\dots,c^{(N)}\): an agent swarm (peers working in parallel) or subagents (helpers a main agent launches and closes) joint outcome held-out benchmarks
Diagnostic (ContextBench) a forced stream of operations \(u_1,\dots,u_n\), each arriving as a new message what survives in the final context (files on disk earn no credit) answers known to the generator
Learning the same tasks; change the skill \(s\) (weights fixed) or the weights \(\theta\) score and compute on held-out data held-out split
Serving recorded CLM workloads server compute at equal accuracy a standard serving engine

ContextBench, the paper’s diagnostic, isolates context management from knowledge and reasoning with four synthetic tasks. Needle Retention: keep 2–8 “needle” lines per ≈4K-token chunk verbatim and discard 140 filler lines. Sudoku Sketchpad: maintain a 16×16 board while single moves stream in, reproducing the exact board after each move. KV Store: absorb batches of 100 records SET key = <24 random words>, then answer 24 GET key queries exactly. Log Triage: absorb batches of service log lines, then answer 24 lookup and counting questions.

Out of scope: new architectures or pretraining, memory carried across separate tasks, wall-clock latency, and formal safety guarantees for edits.

(c) Evaluation metrics

Task score. Accuracy, pass rate, or best evaluator score (higher is better). It shows whether the agent kept the right information.

Prefix-reuse FLOPs (the main cost metric). Shrinking the context saves compute on every later turn, while an edit in the middle destroys the cached computation after it; this metric charges both effects.

Intuition. A server with prefix caching pays (i) a fixed per-token cost for every token it must actually process (uncached prompt tokens plus generated tokens) and (ii) an attention cost per token pair: each newly processed prompt token looks at all tokens before it, and each generated token looks at the whole prompt and the earlier generated tokens.

Formula. At turn \(t\) the prompt has \(P_t\) tokens, of which a prefix of \(R_t\) tokens is reused from the cache, leaving \(U_t = P_t - R_t\) to process; the model generates \(G_t\) tokens:

\[F_t = C_{\text{tok}}\,(U_t + G_t) + C_{\text{att}}\Big[\tfrac12\big(P_t^2 - R_t^2\big) + G_t P_t + \tfrac12 G_t^2\Big], \qquad F = \sum_{t=1}^{T} F_t .\]

The bracket counts token pairs: \(\tfrac12(P_t^2-R_t^2)\) while prefilling the uncached part, \(G_tP_t + \tfrac12 G_t^2\) while decoding. The constants: \(C_{\text{tok}} \approx 2\times\)(weights touched per token), because each weight performs one multiply-add (2 FLOPs) per token; and

\[C_{\text{att}} = 4\,L_{\text{att}}\,h_q\,d_h,\]

because each token pair costs, in each of the \(L_{\text{att}}\) full-attention layers, each of the \(h_q\) query heads, and each of the \(d_h\) head dimensions, one multiply-add for the attention score and one for mixing the values. For Qwen3.6-27B: \(C_{\text{att}} = 4\cdot16\cdot24\cdot256 \approx 3.93\times10^{5}\) and \(C_{\text{tok}} = 4.87\times10^{10}\) (≈24B weights touched per token).

Tiny example. Toy constants \(C_{\text{tok}}=10\), \(C_{\text{att}}=1\); prompt \(P_t=10\), output \(G_t=2\).

  • Append-only turn, \(R_t = 8\): \(10\cdot(2+2) + \big[\tfrac12(100-64) + 20 + 2\big] = 40 + 40 = 80\).
  • Edit at the very start, \(R_t = 0\): \(10\cdot(10+2) + [50+20+2] = 120 + 72 = 192\), i.e., 2.4× more.

At real scale (Qwen3.6-27B, \(P_t = 20{,}000\), \(G_t=500\)), one turn costs \(1.41\times10^{14}\) FLOPs append-only (\(R_t=18{,}000\)), \(5.74\times10^{14}\) after a mid-context edit (\(R_t=10{,}000\)), and \(10.81\times10^{14}\) after an edit at the start (\(R_t=0\)): 7.7× the append-only turn. An edit pays off only when the shorter context saves more on later turns than the recomputation costs now.

Context pressure (ContextBench). Intuition: how many times the total input would fill the context window. Formula:

\[\rho = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} \lvert u_i \rvert}{32{,}768}.\]

Example: 24 Needle-Retention chunks of ≈4K tokens ≈ 96K tokens, so \(\rho \approx 3\); keeping everything is impossible and filler must go. Levels with \(\rho < 1\) are controls where keeping everything fits.

Geometric-mean speedup (Software World). Intuition: the typical multiplicative speed gain across benchmarks, robust to one extreme value. Formula: with \(s_j = \dfrac{\text{CPU instructions executed before}}{\text{CPU instructions executed after}}\) on benchmark \(j\) (a broken benchmark counts as \(s_j = 1\)),

\[S = \Big(\prod_{j=1}^{m} s_j\Big)^{1/m}.\]

Example: \(s_1 = 1.10\), \(s_2 = 1.00\) gives \(S = \sqrt{1.10} \approx 1.049\), a 4.9% speedup. Instruction counts serve as a noise-free proxy for runtime.

Pareto frontier. Intuition: keep only methods that no other method beats on both accuracy and cost. Formula: method \(a\) dominates \(b\) if \(\text{acc}_a \ge \text{acc}_b\) and \(\text{cost}_a \le \text{cost}_b\), with at least one strict; the frontier is the set of undominated methods. Example: \(a = (60\%,\ 6\ \text{PFLOPs})\) dominates \(b = (53\%,\ 8\ \text{PFLOPs})\), so only \(a\) is on the frontier.

For closed models served through paid APIs, cost is reported in USD per task instead of FLOPs.

(d) The standard approach and why it fails

Intuition. A standard LM agent only appends: every action and every tool output goes to the end, and nothing is ever removed.

\[c_{t+1} = c_t \oplus y_t \oplus o_t .\]

Example. At 1,000 tokens per turn, \(\lvert c_{33}\rvert \approx 33{,}000 > 32{,}768\): a 100-turn web search overflows by turn 33.

  • F1 Overflow. The context exceeds \(B\) and the run must stop or be cut.
  • F2 Rising cost and clutter. Per-turn attention cost grows with length, and stale outputs (e.g., irrelevant search results) stay forever.

The usual patch is harness-scheduled compaction: once \(\lvert c_t\rvert > \alpha B\), history is replaced by a summary, \(c_{t+1} = [\text{system prompt},\, x,\, \operatorname{summary}(c_t)]\) (Codex-style uses \(\alpha = 0.75\)). It fixes F1 and introduces:

  • F3 Lossy rewriting. Summaries drop or invent details (exact needle lines, exact Sudoku cells).
  • F4 Fixed timing. Compaction fires at a preset length, not when it is useful.
  • F5 No surgical updates. Changing one Sudoku cell requires regenerating the whole board.
  • F6 No eviction. Text that entered the context can be copied to disk but stays in the live context.
  • F7 Frozen strategy. The policy lives in harness code and cannot improve by learning.

Every editing method also faces:

  • F8 Edits break the cache. An edit at position \(p\) forces recomputation of everything after \(p\) (the 7.7× case above).

(e) Existing baselines

Baseline Who decides when Allowed operation Fixes Remaining limitation
Base (Mini-SWE-Agent: a minimal agent whose only tool is a shell) nobody append only none F1, F2
Codex-style Summary (from OpenAI’s Codex coding agent) harness, at 75% of \(B\) summarize all but the system prompt and task F1 F3, F4, F5, F6
MEM1 harness, every turn rewrite one compact state from the previous state plus the new observation F1, F2 rewrite every turn; F3, F7
Self-Compact model, asked every 2 turns once the context exceeds 37% of \(B\) whole-history summary F4 F3, F5, F6
ACM (Agentic Context Management) model replace everything since its previous call with a summary; query the originals later F4, partly F3 fixed granularity; F5
Context Folding model branch into a sub-task and return only its summary keeps sub-task clutter out cannot delete from the main context (F6)
RLM (Recursive Language Model) model, through code the long input lives as a variable in a code interpreter, read on demand huge inputs never flood the context the live history still only grows (F1, F2)

Down this list the model gains more control, always within an operation set designed by humans.

(f) The method: Context Language Models

One-sentence idea. Mirror the model’s live context into an ordinary file and let the model rewrite that file with any code, so context management becomes the model’s own behavior rather than harness logic.

Analogy. A standard agent writes in a bound notebook with a pen and can only add pages. A CLM works on a whiteboard: it erases dead ends, condenses a messy area into a clean note, keeps a scoreboard it updates in place, and photographs a section into a drawer (disk) before erasing it.

Component 1: model-controlled transition. Intuition: the model’s output may contain a small program that rewrites its own next context; without one, the system appends as usual.

\[c_{t+1} = g_t\big(c_t \oplus y_t \oplus o_t\big), \qquad g_t = \begin{cases} \text{the edit program written in } y_t & \text{if the model edits},\\ \text{identity (plain append)} & \text{otherwise}. \end{cases}\]

The paper writes this compactly as \(c_{t+1} = f^{\text{CLM}}_\theta(c_t)\), versus \(c_{t+1} = c_t \oplus f^{\text{LM}}_\theta(c_t)\) for a standard LM. Example: the context holds a 200-token task, three 3,000-token search results, and a 100-token note (\(\lvert c\rvert = 9{,}300\)). The model writes a Python loop replacing each irrelevant result by “Searched X: no relevant results” (≈20 tokens), leaving \(\lvert c\rvert \approx 200 + 60 + 100 = 360\).

Component 2: context as a file. The live context sits at a path such as /tmp/.live_ctx/LIVE_CTX_MAIN.txt, named in the system prompt. The model edits it with ordinary shell tools (sed, grep, Python). After each command the harness reloads the file, so the edited text is exactly what the server receives next. Two light supports remain in the harness: a reminder appears 2,048 tokens before the budget (current models estimate their own context length poorly), and on some benchmarks a turn that would overflow is rolled back and retried.

Component 3: multi-agent through more files. A swarm starts with one context file per agent; a subagent is launched by creating a context file and ended by deleting it. An orchestrator can keep a compact scoreboard of its workers inside its own file.

Component 4: steering with a skill. Intuition: because management is the model’s own behavior, plain instructions change it.

\[y_t \sim \pi_\theta(\cdot \mid c_t,\ s).\]

Example: \(s =\) “Whenever your context exceeds 24,000 tokens, compact it to about 4,000.” The first compaction then occurs at a median of ≈23.6K tokens.

Component 5: evolving the skill. Intuition: with the model fixed, search over instruction texts and keep the one that scores best.

\[s^\star = \arg\max_{s}\ \mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{D}}\big[\,r(\tau(x;s))\,\big],\]

where \(\tau(x;s)\) is the trajectory (full record of turns) the agent produces on task \(x\) with skill \(s\), and \(\mathcal{D}\) is the task distribution. A proposer LM reads rollouts (including a success and a failure on the same instance) and writes candidate skills; each candidate is screened on 6, then 12 more training instances, then scored on a development split; skills that are Pareto-optimal in accuracy and cost are kept; the final pick is tested once on a held-out split. The proposer is either a stronger model (assisted evolution) or the agent itself (self-evolution). Example: on KV Store the empty skill scores 22.3% on the development split and the evolved skill 83.8%, so the evolved skill is selected.

Component 6: RL with a success-gated efficiency bonus.

6a. Outcome advantage. Intuition: in GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization), the model makes \(n\) attempts at the same question, and each attempt is scored relative to its group, so no separate value-estimating network is needed.

\[A^{\text{out}}_i = \frac{r_i - \operatorname{mean}(r_{1:n})}{\operatorname{std}(r_{1:n})}.\]

Example: rewards \((1,1,0,0)\) give mean \(0.5\), std \(0.5\), so \(A^{\text{out}} = (1,\,1,\,-1,\,-1)\).

6b. Efficiency advantage. Intuition: among successful attempts, reward the cheaper ones; failures earn no efficiency credit, so the model cannot gain by deleting context recklessly.

\[A^{\text{eff}}_i = \begin{cases} \operatorname{clip}\!\Big(\dfrac{\bar c - c_i}{\bar c},\,-1,\,1\Big) & i \in \mathcal{S},\\ 0 & i \notin \mathcal{S}, \end{cases} \qquad \bar c = \frac{1}{\lvert\mathcal{S}\rvert}\sum_{k\in\mathcal{S}} c_k ,\]

where \(\mathcal{S}\) is the set of successful attempts, \(c_i\) is attempt \(i\)’s prefix-reuse FLOPs, and \(A^{\text{eff}} \equiv 0\) whenever \(\lvert\mathcal{S}\rvert < 2\). Example: the two successes cost 2 and 4 PFLOPs, so \(\bar c = 3\) and \(A^{\text{eff}} = (+\tfrac13,\ -\tfrac13,\ 0,\ 0)\).

6c. Combination.

\[A_i = A^{\text{out}}_i + w\,A^{\text{eff}}_i, \qquad w = 0.25 .\]

Example: \(A = (1.083,\ 0.917,\ -1,\ -1)\): both successes are reinforced, the cheaper one more.

6d. Stepwise update. Intuition: edits rewrite the past, so a trajectory is not one growing sequence; every model call \(j\) of attempt \(i\) is trained on the exact context \(c_{i,j}\) it saw, weighted by its attempt’s advantage.

\[\nabla_\theta J \approx \sum_{i=1}^{n} A_i \sum_{j} \nabla_\theta \log \pi_\theta\big(y_{i,j} \mid c_{i,j}\big).\]

Example: an attempt with \(A_i = 1.083\) and three model calls makes all three outputs more likely with the same weight \(1.083\). The implementation adds ratio clipping in \([0.2,\,0.28]\) (a cap on how far one update moves each probability), a KL penalty of 0.01 (keeping the model close to its starting point), and applies the efficiency term to context-management tokens.

Component 7: Suffix Cache Reuse (SCR), a serving co-design. Intuition: after an edit \([X\,Y\,Z] \to [X\,Y'\,Z]\), the span \(Z\) is unchanged text, so its cached keys and values are reused; only \(Y'\) is new.

\[\text{recomputed tokens:}\quad \underbrace{\lvert Y'\rvert + \lvert Z\rvert}_{\text{standard prefix caching}} \;\longrightarrow\; \underbrace{\lvert Y'\rvert}_{\text{SCR}} .\]

\(Z\) shifts by \(\Delta = \lvert Y'\rvert - \lvert Y\rvert\) positions. Because RoPE encodes position as a rotation, moving a cached key is one extra rotation, \(k \leftarrow \mathcal{R}(\Delta)\,k\). Example: \(X\) = 10,000 tokens, \(Y\) = 5,000 tokens of search results replaced by a 200-token note \(Y'\), \(Z\) = 3,000 tokens. Standard serving recomputes 3,200 tokens; SCR computes 200 and rotates \(Z\)’s keys by \(\Delta = -4{,}800\).

SCR is an approximation: \(Z\)’s cached states were computed while \(Z\) attended to the old \(Y\). To bound it, at most \(K = 6\) surviving spans (the longest) are relocated per edit and the rest are recomputed. Linear-attention layers hold no per-token cache, so SCR continues from their pre-edit state snapshot, and \(Y'\) is processed only in the 16 full-attention layers. The same mechanism serves ordinary chat traffic: reasoning models’ chat templates delete earlier hidden “thinking” blocks every turn, which is itself an edit.

Pseudocode.

# ---- CLM agent loop (a swarm runs one loop per context file) ----
ctx = File("/tmp/.live_ctx/LIVE_CTX_MAIN.txt")
ctx.write(system_prompt(path=ctx.path) + skill s + task x)
for t in 1..T:
    c = ctx.read()
    if tokens(c) > B - 2048: c += "[near budget: consider editing your context]"
    y = LM(c)                          # reasoning + one shell command
    o = run(y.command)                 # the command may rewrite ctx (sed, python, ...)
    if ctx was not modified:
        ctx.append(y + o)              # default: plain append
    # if it was modified, the edited file itself is the next context
    if y.done: break

# ---- RL: stepwise GRPO with success-gated efficiency ----
for step in 1..70:
    for each of 8 prompts:
        run n = 32 CLM attempts, saving every (c_ij, y_ij)
        r_i = judge(answer_i) in {0,1};   cost_i = prefix-reuse FLOPs of attempt i
        A_i = A_out_i + 0.25 * A_eff_i
    drop groups whose rewards are all equal          # no learning signal
    policy-gradient step on every (c_ij -> y_ij), weighted by A_i

# ---- Serving with SCR ----
on each new prompt of a session:
    diff against the session's previous prompt
    reuse the cached prefix X
    relocate up to K = 6 surviving spans (re-rotate their RoPE keys)
    prefill only new or changed tokens

How the pieces fix each failure.

Failure Fix in CLMs
F1 Overflow the model compresses or deletes before reaching \(B\); reminder at \(B - 2{,}048\)
F2 Cost and clutter stale outputs are deleted, keeping the live context small (an orchestrator stays at 6–8K tokens)
F3 Lossy rewriting exact text stays verbatim, backups go to disk, notes record what was removed
F4 Fixed timing the model decides when, and a skill can tell it when
F5 No surgical updates a one-line sed changes one Sudoku cell
F6 No eviction any span can be deleted, including input already read
F7 Frozen strategy skills, skill evolution, and RL improve management
F8 Edits break the cache the RL efficiency bonus favors cache-friendly edits; SCR reuses the unchanged suffix

4. Results and analysis

Organization. The experiments answer three questions in sequence. Part A asks whether an existing LM, simply handed an editable context file, already manages context better than human-designed strategies (zero-shot). Part B asks whether that management improves through learning, in the context (instructions, evolved skills) or in the weights (RL). Part C asks whether serving can recover the compute that edits cost (failure F8). General setup: within each comparison every method uses the same LM, the same agent backbone (a minimal shell-only agent; the Pi agent harness for the 24-hour swarm), and the same token budget (mostly 32K, counted with OpenAI’s o200k tokenizer), and differs only in context management. Costs in Parts A and B assume standard prefix caching; SCR’s extra savings appear only in Part C. How to read: most plots put cost (prefix-reuse PFLOPs per question, Section 3c; lower is better) on the x-axis and task score (higher is better) on the y-axis, so the best point sits top-left, and a dashed Pareto frontier joins the undominated methods. In tables, ↑ means higher is better and ↓ lower is better. Numbers marked ≈ are read off figures.

Part A: Does an off-the-shelf model manage its own context better than fixed strategies?

Setup. The comparison climbs three tiers of horizon. Diagnostic: ContextBench with GPT-5.4 at 32K, pressure \(\rho\) from 0.25× to 24×, 4–8 seeds (independent random runs) per level; every method gets the same task instruction plus an equally detailed skill for its own mechanism. Short horizon (≤100 turns): Qwen3.6-27B (an open 27-billion-parameter model) at 32K on TerminalBench 2.1 (89 terminal tasks with pass/fail test scripts), TBLite (a lighter terminal benchmark), and BrowseComp-Plus (830 hard research questions answered by searching a fixed document collection and graded by an LLM judge), against the six baselines of Section 3e. Long horizon: four math optimization problems (circle packing, min–max distance ratio, Erdős minimum overlap, Heilbronn triangles) with Claude 4.6 Sonnet against OpenEvolve (an evolutionary program-search system modeled on DeepMind’s AlphaEvolve) and OpenEvolve-Agent, capped at 100 scored attempts or 5 hours, one run each; EdgeBench-10 (ten real code-optimization tasks, 12 hours each, best of three seeds, judge score 0–100) with Qwen3.6-27B and Claude 4.6 Sonnet against Summary; and Software World, where six GPT-5.6-Sol agents (272K budget) spend over 24 hours speeding up six interdependent Python libraries (requests, urllib3, and four packages built on them) and are scored by geometric-mean speedup on 17 benchmarks from four downstream packages they never see.

How to read. ContextBench plots accuracy against pressure: a flat line at 1.0 is perfect, and a falling line marks where a strategy breaks. Short-horizon plots are accuracy vs prefix-reuse PFLOPs (top-left wins). Long-horizon results report final best score, with compute per trial in PF (prefix-reuse PFLOPs) where measured.

Takeaway 1: Letting the model edit its own context beats every fixed strategy in score while using less compute, from synthetic diagnostics to 24-hour multi-agent runs.

  • Diagnostic. CLM stays at ≈1.0 on all four tasks at every pressure, while the best baseline falls to ≈0.35–0.75 at the highest pressure. The failure modes match Section 3d: summaries drop needles and corrupt Sudoku boards (F3), methods without in-place edits regenerate whole boards (F5), and offloading tools store data on disk without evicting it (F6).
  • Short horizon. On BrowseComp-Plus, CLM reaches 59.4% (11.4% relative above Summary) with 21.5% fewer PFLOPs than Summary and 28.9% fewer than MEM1. It matches Summary on TerminalBench 2.1 with 29.5% fewer PFLOPs and beats it on TBLite (73.7% vs 67.0%) at 91% of its PFLOPs, lying on the Pareto frontier of all three.
  • Long horizon. CLM leads all four math problems; on EdgeBench-10 it scores 44.6 vs 42.3 with 59% less compute (Qwen3.6-27B) and 51.0 vs 42.3 (Claude 4.6 Sonnet); in Software World its swarm reaches ≈1.044× vs ≈1.026× at equal spend, a 65% larger gain.
  • Model capability drives the gain. Qwen3.5-9B edits 1.4 times per TerminalBench task (none in half of them) versus 2.6 for Qwen3.6-27B, and its median peak context is 30.2K vs 17.6K tokens; it still edges Summary on BrowseComp-Plus (39.9% vs 37.7%).
  • Subagents help when there is room. At 32K, CLM with subagents ties plain CLM on EdgeBench-10 (44.2 vs 44.6); at 128K, subagents lead (50.2 vs 47.3 for CLM and 47.8 for Summary, at 219 / 142 / 222 PF per trial).
  • New behaviors emerge unprompted. An orchestrator updates a worker scoreboard through 163 in-place edits while staying at 6–8K tokens; the model invents a “notes” chat role; it defines a compact_turns helper and reuses it 37 times.

Part B: Can context management be taught, in context or in weights?

Setup. Three levers. Talking (Component 4): Claude 4.6 Sonnet on BrowseComp-Plus, one sentence appended to the task prompt versus no sentence on the same questions: “compact to ≈4K once your context exceeds \(Y\)” for \(Y \in \{16\text{K}, 24\text{K}, 32\text{K}\}\); “compact only at sub-question boundaries” (sessions of four chained questions); “back up the context file to disk before every edit.” Evolving instructions (Component 5): on ContextBench at 32K, assisted evolution pairs a Qwen3.6-27B agent that starts with no context-management instruction with Claude Fable 5.1 as skill proposer; self-evolution uses Claude Opus 5 for both roles; cost is PFLOPs per task for Qwen and USD per task for Opus. Training weights (Component 6): Qwen3.5-9B trained for 70 GRPO steps on 3,040 OpenResearcher research prompts (8 prompts × 32 attempts per step, efficiency weight 0.25), then tested on all 830 BrowseComp-Plus questions; the Summary harness trained with the same recipe (task reward only) is the control.

How to read. For talking, the measured behavior should track the instruction (first compaction near \(Y\), compaction spiking at boundaries, backups appearing). For evolution, good skills move up (accuracy) and left (cost) from the starting point. For RL, compare before → after accuracy (↑) and PFLOPs per question (↓).

Takeaway 2: Context management is a learnable skill: one sentence reliably reshapes it, evolved instructions repair weak management, and RL turns a small model from worse than Summary into equally accurate at 39% less compute.

  • Talking works. First compaction lands at ≈16.0K / ≈23.6K / ≈30.9K tokens for \(Y\) = 16K / 24K / 32K; compaction exactly at a sub-question boundary rises from ≈0.34 to ≈0.77; edits preceded by a full backup rise from ≈0.00 to ≈0.68. Harness and weights stay unchanged.
  • Evolving works. Assisted evolution lifts development accuracy on all four tasks (KV Store 22.3% → 83.8%, Log Triage 0.0% → 100%), and on the held-out KV Store test split from 38.3% to 74.2% (+35.9 points), with evolved skills extending the accuracy–cost Pareto frontier. Under self-evolution, Opus 5 starts at 94–100% and its evolved skills cut cost or raise accuracy further.
  • Training works. RL lifts CLM from 28.8% to 42.5% (+47.6% relative) while PFLOPs per question fall from 1.52 to 1.34 (−12%). The trained Summary harness reaches 42.1% at 2.19 PFLOPs, so CLM ends 0.4 points ahead with 38.8% fewer PFLOPs. The efficiency bonus lowers cost without a clear accuracy loss.

Part C: Can serving recover the compute that edits cost?

Setup. As Section 3c shows, an edit near the start of a 20K-token prompt makes a turn 7.7× more expensive under standard prefix caching. The test serves Qwen3.6-27B CLM runs on all 830 BrowseComp-Plus questions with standard SGLang (an open-source LLM serving engine with prefix caching) and with SGLang plus SCR (\(K = 6\)). A sweep over \(K \in \{1, 2, 3, 6, 12, 64\}\) on 64 questions checks sensitivity.

How to read. Accuracy should stay equal while PFLOPs per question fall. The token breakdown splits every prompt token into served from the prefix cache, reused by SCR, or recomputed; less recomputation means less waste, and “edited turns” isolates the turns right after an edit.

Takeaway 3: SCR cuts server compute by 35% at identical accuracy, and most of its saving also applies to ordinary reasoning-model serving.

  • Same accuracy, less compute. Both systems score ≈60.2%; SCR needs 65.0% of standard SGLang’s compute (≈10.98 → ≈7.14 PFLOPs per question).
  • Where the saving comes from. SCR reuses 7.8% of all prompt tokens beyond prefix-cache hits: 5.3 points after deleted reasoning blocks and 2.5 points after CLM edits. In edited turns, recomputed tokens drop from ≈75.8% to ≈41.8%.
  • Robust to \(K\). Accuracy shows no degradation for any \(K\), and relocated tokens per edit saturate around \(K = 6\) (≈4K tokens).
  • Remaining waste is fixable. In edited turns ≈22.7% of prompt tokens are an unchanged prefix that SGLang still recomputes, because it stores linear-attention states only at request boundaries; checkpointing states at message boundaries targets this.
Serving Accuracy ↑ PFLOPs / question ↓ All turns: cached / SCR-reused / recomputed (% tokens) Edited turns: cached / SCR-reused / recomputed
Standard SGLang ≈60.2% ≈10.98 ≈72.9 / 0 / ≈27.1 ≈24.2 / 0 / ≈75.8
SGLang + SCR (\(K=6\)) ≈60.2% ≈7.14 (65.0%) ≈73.9 / 7.8 / ≈18.3 ≈29.9 / ≈28.2 / ≈41.8

5. Limitations

Unrestricted self-editing removes guarantees about what the model keeps. A CLM can delete task constraints, overwrite the record of its own actions, or write instructions to itself that persist into later turns (a prompt injection, i.e., text that steers a model toward unintended instructions); the paper cites a documented case of a model planting unauthorized instructions in its own compaction summary. After many edits, the live context no longer serves as an audit trail of what happened. The paper names this risk but evaluates no injection resistance, no faithfulness of edited history, and no safeguards such as write-protected regions or edit logs, and every reported number comes from benign tasks. Settings where instructions must hold, such as security policies or user constraints, need these safeguards before CLMs are deployed.

The comparisons carry small CLM-specific allowances, and several headline gains rest on few runs. On BrowseComp-Plus, CLM’s editing turns do not count toward the 100-turn cap and an overflowing turn can be rolled back and retried up to six times, allowances stated only for CLM; in RL, CLM likewise gets 80 non-editing turns. ContextBench is the authors’ own benchmark, and its prompts explicitly say “delete this entire block” or “offload this whole block,” operations that only an editable context can perform. The math results use one run per method, Software World one swarm per method with a 1.8-point absolute difference (1.044× vs 1.026×), and EdgeBench reports best-of-three without spread. Models, judges, and budgets also change between sections: Qwen3.5-9B with CLM scores 39.9% vs 37.7% for Summary on BrowseComp-Plus in the zero-shot comparison, but 28.8% vs 34.7% in the RL setting.

“CLM” is a harness pattern plus training, and its efficiency claims rely on proxies and approximations. Zero-shot CLM is an existing LM with a file-sync wrapper, a budget reminder, and rollback; no new architecture is involved, and the benefit shrinks with weaker models (Qwen3.5-9B edits half as often and fills its context to 30.2K of 32K). Learning in the weights is shown for one 9B model, one task family, and 70 RL steps. Cost is theoretical prefix-reuse FLOPs or USD, not wall-clock latency. SCR recovers editing costs only approximately: reused suffix states are stale, linear-attention layers never see the new text, accuracy is checked for one model on one benchmark (64 questions for the \(K\) sweep), and most of its saving (5.3 of 7.8 points) comes from deleted reasoning blocks rather than from CLM edits.

6. How to reproduce

Step 1: Get the code, models, and hardware. The official repository is github.com/facebookresearch/context-language-models (CC BY-NC 4.0, non-commercial). It contains clm/clm_harness (CLM inside Harbor, an agent-evaluation framework: pip install -e ., then clm-harbor run -p <harbor-task> -a clm-minimal -m openai/<model> --agent-kwarg api_base=http://localhost:8000/v1), clm/clm_icl (skill evolution), clm/clm_rl (RL), and suffix_cache_reuse (the SGLang patch); a pi-clm plugin for the Pi agent installs with pi install npm:@lolipopshock/pi-clm. Open-weight models (Qwen3.6-27B, Qwen3.5-9B) are served with vLLM for evaluation and SGLang for RL rollouts and SCR (both open-source LLM serving engines). Closed models come through paid APIs: GPT-5.4, GPT-5.4-nano (RL judge), GPT-5.6-Sol, Claude 4.6 Sonnet, Claude Fable 5.1, and Claude Opus 5. RL used 16 H200 GPUs for the policy and 48 for rollouts.

Step 2: Configure the CLM harness. Use a minimal shell-only agent (Mini-SWE-Agent style; Pi for Software World). Mirror the context to /tmp/.live_ctx/LIVE_CTX_MAIN.txt, name the path in the system prompt, reload the file after every command, and append by default. Insert the budget reminder 2,048 tokens before the limit and count tokens with the o200k tokenizer. On BrowseComp-Plus, exclude editing turns from the 100-turn cap and allow up to six rollback-and-retry attempts on overflow; on EdgeBench all methods roll back up to 50 times. Expose BrowseComp-Plus search tools as in-context skills. Subagents are capped at five (40 turns each) for math and five to six for EdgeBench.

Step 3: Prepare benchmarks and baselines. ContextBench: GPT-5.4, 32,768-token limit with 2,048 reserved for output, 4 seeds (8 on selected levels), the same task instruction plus a per-method skill. TerminalBench 2.1: 89 tasks, thinking (hidden reasoning) on, 4,096 generated tokens per call, 32,000-token budget, 64 turns, 180 s per command, 4× default time limit; TBLite: same with 2,048 generated tokens per call. BrowseComp-Plus: 830 questions, top-10 snippets of 512 tokens, document reader capped at 8,192 tokens, temperature 0.7, top-p 0.95, 23,560-token budget, Qwen3.5-27B as judge at temperature 0. Math: Claude 4.6 Sonnet, 32,000 tokens, 100 attempts or 5 hours; OpenEvolve with population 60 in four islands; OpenEvolve-Agent with 25 turns per candidate. EdgeBench-10: tasks ad_placement_optimization, apple_incremental_game, graph_node_classification, grid_turing_robot, juliet_vulnerability_analyzer, openrct2_theme_park_ai, schemathesis_datagen_pipeline, triangulation_coloring_optimization, vehicle_routing_time_windows, wesnoth_tactical_ai; 3 seeds, 12 hours, no network, temperature 0.7, 8,192 generated tokens, 32,000 budget (128,000 for the extra study). Software World: agents on requests, urllib3, nilearn, requests-gssapi, databricks-sql-connector, responses; held-out requests-cache, cachecontrol, zeep, awswrangler; GPT-5.6-Sol at 272K; cost in USD. Baselines: Summary uses the Codex prompts at 75% of budget; Self-Compact its original prompts every two turns past 37%; RLM and ACM their released code; MEM1 the authors’ re-implementation.

Step 4: Compute the metrics. Apply the prefix-reuse FLOPs formula of Section 3c turn by turn. Qwen3.6-27B constants: 64 layers, hidden size 5,120, MLP width 17,408; 16 full-attention layers with 24 query heads, 4 key–value heads, head dimension 256; 48 Gated DeltaNet layers with 16 key heads, 48 value heads, head dimensions 128. Evaluation matches cached prefixes at message level; RL uses exact token-level matching against the previous turn. Software World speedup uses executed-instruction counts on 17 CPU benchmarks.

Step 5: Run the learning experiments. Steering prompts appear verbatim in the paper’s Appendix E (thresholds: 30 long questions, 48K budget, 200 turns; boundaries: 189 sessions of four questions, 24K budget; backup: 200 questions, 16K budget). Skill evolution (clm/clm_icl) is a GEPA-style loop (reflective prompt evolution): four parallel proposers, each reading at least ten rollouts and writing at least four full rewrites; screening on 6 then 12 training instances; development split of 102 instances per task; a lineage stops after five non-improving proposals; the test split has 102 instances × 3 seeds; the agent runs at 32,000 tokens, 4,096 reserved, 240 turns. RL (clm/clm_rl): 3,040 OpenResearcher prompts, 8 prompts × 32 rollouts per step, learning rate \(10^{-6}\), weight decay 0.1, clipping \([0.2, 0.28]\), KL coefficient 0.01, truncated importance sampling (a correction for rollouts produced by a slightly stale model copy), dynamic sampling (dropping groups with identical rewards), 70 steps, temperature 0.7, top-p 0.95; CLM at 28K budget with 2,048 reserved and 80 non-editing turns; Summary compacts at 28,672 tokens with 100 turns; binary reward from GPT-5.4-nano with the DeepSearchQA rubric; \(w = 0.25\); checkpoint chosen on 500 held-out OpenResearcher questions.

Step 6: Measure serving with SCR. Apply the suffix_cache_reuse patch to SGLang with \(K = 6\) and session-private cache slots, serve Qwen3.6-27B CLM runs on all 830 BrowseComp-Plus questions, and compare accuracy, PFLOPs per question, and the token breakdown against unpatched SGLang; repeat on 64 questions for \(K \in \{1,2,3,6,12,64\}\).

Missing parts. ContextBench is marked “coming soon” in the repository, and Software World (library versions, the 17 benchmarks, the wake schedule between work sessions) has no listed release. The full CLM system prompt and per-method skills appear only as excerpts. RL details left open: the exact advantage normalization, the size of the penalties for failed tool calls and malformed outputs, and how the efficiency term is restricted to context-management tokens. Seeds and Qwen3.5-9B FLOPs constants are not listed. Some settings differ across the paper: TerminalBench 2.1 uses 64 turns in the appendix versus a 100-turn cap in the main figure; BrowseComp-Plus is labeled 32K but configured with a 23,560-token budget; EdgeBench subagents are capped at five in the main text and six in the appendix; the BrowseComp-Plus judge is Qwen3.5-27B for zero-shot runs and GPT-5.4-nano for RL. Several experiments require paid access to closed models.
